title: C'è e Ci Sono
subtitle: "There is" and "there are" — your first taste of the particle ci.
objectives: Use c'è for singular and ci sono for plural existence
Form the negative and question forms
Recognize ci as "here/there" in this fixed expression

content.intro: C'è and ci sono are how Italian says "there is" and "there are" — useful from your very first day, for describing a room, a menu, or a city.
content.explanation: C'è is a contraction of ci (here/there) + è (is); ci sono is ci + sono (are). You'll meet ci again properly at B1 as a full pronoun/particle — for now, just learn c'è/ci sono as a fixed pair, matching singular vs. plural exactly like essere itself does.

rules.heading: a) Affirmative
rules.body:
• c'è + singular noun: C'è un bar qui vicino.
  • ci sono + plural noun: Ci sono due bar qui vicino.

rules.heading: b) Negative
rules.body:
• Non c'è tempo. (There isn't time.)
  • Non ci sono problemi. (There aren't [any] problems.)

rules.heading: c) Question
rules.body:
• C'è latte in frigo? (Is there milk in the fridge?)
  • Ci sono posti liberi? (Are there free seats?)

examples.it: C'è un ristorante molto buono qui vicino.
examples.en: There's a very good restaurant near here.

examples.it: Ci sono tre camere da letto.
Quante persone ci sono alla festa?
examples.en: How many people are there at the party?

examples.it: C'è un problema con il tuo biglietto.
examples.en: There's a problem with your ticket.

commonMistakes.why: A plural noun (due gatti) needs the plural ci sono, not the singular c'è.
"There is a problem" needs c'è, not just è — plain è means "[it] is", not "there is".

items.explanation: Plural camere needs ci sono, not c'è.

items.prompt: Which is correct: "there are many students"?
items.explanation: Plural molti studenti needs ci sono.

items.prompt: Which form goes with a plural noun?
"C'è latte in frigo?" is asking about...
items.explanation: Latte (milk) is treated as singular here, so c'è is used.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses ci sono?
items.explanation: Ci sono needs a plural noun, like due problemi.

items.prompt: What does the "ci" in c'è/ci sono originally mean?
items.explanation: Ci originally means "here/there", the core of this fixed expression.

items.statement: C'è is used with plural nouns.
items.explanation: C'è is used with singular nouns; ci sono is for plurals.

items.statement: "Ci sono due camere" is grammatically correct.
items.explanation: Due camere is plural, matching ci sono.

items.statement: The negative of c'è is formed by adding non before it.
items.explanation: Non c'è / non ci sono are the standard negatives.

items.statement: C'è and ci sono only differ by verb tense, not number.
items.explanation: They differ by number (singular vs. plural), not tense — both are present tense.

items.statement: The "ci" in this fixed expression will reappear later as a fuller pronoun/particle at B1.
items.explanation: Ci is introduced properly as a particle at B1.

items.statement: "È un problema" and "c'è un problema" mean exactly the same thing.
items.explanation: È means "[it] is"; c'è means "there is" — different meanings.

summary: C'è = there is (singular); ci sono = there are (plural).
Negate with non c'è / non ci sono; question by intonation or word order, same as any yes/no question.
You'll meet ci again as a full particle at B1 — for now, treat c'è/ci sono as one fixed pair.
